lede: There is no dividing by a matrix. Instead there is an inverse: the matrix that undoes what the first one did. For a two by two matrix it takes one number and three actions, and none of it is printed on your formula sheet.
can: Work out a determinant, sign and all.
Build an inverse by swapping, negating and dividing, then check it.
Say when a matrix has no inverse, and name the matrix.

md: Multiply a number by 4 and you undo it by multiplying by $\frac{1}{4}$. A matrix is undone by its **inverse**, written $A^{-1}$: multiplied together, the two give the **identity**, the matrix with 1s on the leading diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Multiplying by the identity changes nothing, just as multiplying by 1 does.

title: Why there is no dividing
md: Matrix multiplication depends on the order, so a fraction bar could not say which side to divide on. The inverse does the undoing instead, and the way to test one is to multiply back and look for the identity.

stem: Show that $\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ is the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

steps.decision: Each entry of the product is a row of the first matrix times a column of the second.
Off the leading diagonal, the products cancel.
The second row finishes the pattern.
Reaching the identity proves it is the inverse; the same multiplication checks any inverse you find.

prompt: Which matrix is the inverse of $P = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$? Check by multiplying.
explain: Multiply as in the See it. Row 1 of $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ by the columns of $P$ gives $4 - 3 = 1$ and $6 - 6 = 0$; row 2 gives 0 and 1. The product is the identity.

twin.prompt: Which matrix is the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$? Check by multiplying.
twin.explain: Its rows times the columns give $5 - 4 = 1$, $2 - 2 = 0$, $-10 + 10 = 0$ and $-4 + 5 = 1$: the identity.

optionNotes.why: That is the matrix itself; squared, it gives 29 in the top-left corner, not 1.
Changing every sign gives the negative of the matrix, which does not undo it.
That is P itself. Multiplying P by P gives 7 in the top-left corner, not the 1 of the identity.
Changing every sign does not undo P: its first row times the first column of P gives −7, not 1.

md: Every inverse starts with one number, the **determinant**. For $\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ it is $ad - bc$: the leading diagonal's product, take away the other diagonal's. Write it on its own line with every product in brackets, so that a negative entry keeps its sign.

steps.decision: The leading diagonal first, then take away the other diagonal, each product in brackets.
The determinant is negative, and that sign has to survive into the inverse.

explain: As in the See it: $(-2)(-4) - (5)(3) = 8 - 15 = -7$. The two negatives on the leading diagonal multiply to a positive, and the answer keeps its minus sign.

md: With the determinant found, the inverse takes three actions in order. **Swap** the leading diagonal, so $a$ and $d$ change places. **Negate** the other diagonal, so $b$ and $c$ change sign. **Divide** every entry by the determinant; the factor may stay outside the brackets.

steps.decision: Determinant first, on its own line.
Swap 5 and 2 on the leading diagonal; change the signs of 3 and 2.
Divide every entry by 4; leaving $\frac{1}{4}$ outside the brackets is accepted.

title: Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix - Corbettmaths
why: The same three actions on more matrices. Pause before the division and write the factor yourself.

prompt: Find the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is 1.
explain: As in the See it: swap 3 and 2, change the signs of 5 and 1, then divide by the determinant, 1, which changes nothing. So the inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

twin.prompt: Find the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is 2.
twin.explain: Swap 4 and 2, change the signs of 2 and 3, then divide every entry by the determinant, 2.

optionNotes.why: Swapped and negated, then never divided by the determinant, 2.
The signs changed and the factor is right, but 4 and 2 never swapped.
The signs changed, but 3 and 2 on the leading diagonal never swapped places.
The leading diagonal swapped, but 5 and 1 kept their signs; the other diagonal changes sign.

text: A negative determinant keeps its sign

md: When the determinant is negative, the factor in front is negative too: a determinant of $-10$ gives $\frac{1}{-10}$. Drop that minus sign and every entry of the inverse changes sign, so the check by multiplying gives $-1$s where the 1s should be.

title: One minus sign, four entries
md: The Summer 2025 inverse was very well answered, and the slips the report named were reciprocals written without the minus sign of a negative determinant. Put the determinant in the factor in brackets, sign and all.

steps.decision: The other diagonal's product is the larger, so the determinant is negative.
Swap and negate exactly as before.
The factor carries the determinant's minus sign.

explain: As in the See it, the factor is one over the determinant with its sign, $\frac{1}{-6}$. Swapping 2 and 1 and negating 4 and 2 gives $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.

twin.explain: The factor is $\frac{1}{-7}$, sign kept; swapping 3 and 1 and negating 2 and 5 gives $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -5 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

optionNotes.why: The determinant's minus sign is missing from the factor.
That multiplies by the determinant instead of dividing by it.
The minus sign of the determinant has gone from the factor, so every entry would come out with its sign turned over.
That multiplies by the determinant; the inverse divides by it, so the factor is its reciprocal.

text: No inverse when the determinant is 0

md: The inverse divides by the determinant, and nothing can be divided by 0. So a matrix whose determinant is 0 has **no inverse**, and it is called **singular**. When a question asks why an equation cannot be solved, name the matrix as well as giving the reason.

steps.working: $\det T = 0$, so $T$ is singular and has no inverse
steps.decision: Name the matrix as well as the reason: the 2023 report found answers that never said which matrix it was.

prompt: Which answer explains why $V = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 4 \\ 9 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse?
options: $\det V = 0$, so $V$ is singular and has no inverse
answer: $\det V = 0$, so $V$ is singular and has no inverse
explain: As in the See it: $\det V = (6)(6) - (4)(9) = 0$, so $V$ is singular. The answer names $V$ and gives the zero determinant as the reason.

twin.explain: $\det W = 20 - 20 = 0$, so $W$ has no inverse: name $W$ and give the zero determinant.

optionNotes.why: That repeats the question without the reason or the name: give det W = 0 and name W.
The two products were added; subtracted they give 0.
True, but it never says which matrix: the full answer names V as the matrix with no inverse.
That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts them, $36 - 36 = 0$, and a non-zero determinant would mean an inverse exists.

md: **Part (i), then used.** (2024, 2025) The inverse is a 2-mark first part, and later parts multiply by it to solve an equation, so the marks that follow rest on it.

**The first step of a matrix equation.** (2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2026) The inverse undoes the matrix in front of the unknown; in 2018 the matrix to invert was itself a difference of two matrices, worked out first.

**A letter that makes it singular.** (2021) A matrix with a letter has no inverse for one value: set its determinant equal to 0 and solve. In 2023 an equation could not be solved because a named matrix was singular.

stem: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}k & 3 \\ 8 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse. Find $k$.

steps.decision: No inverse means the determinant is 0: write it with the letter in.

prompt: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3 & k \\ 4 & 12\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse. Find $k$.
explain: As in the See it, set the determinant to 0: $(3)(12) - 4k = 0$, so $36 = 4k$ and $k = 9$.

twin.prompt: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5 & k \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse. Find $k$.

md:
Work out a determinant as $ad - bc$, each product in brackets.
Build an inverse: swap, negate, then divide every entry by the determinant.
Keep the minus sign of a negative determinant in the factor.
Say that a matrix with determinant 0 is singular, and name it.
Check an inverse by multiplying back to the identity.

Finding an inverse is usually part (i) of a longer matrix question, worth 2 marks: one for the determinant, one for the finished inverse with its factor. Later parts use it, so check it by multiplying back. Stuck? Write $\det = ad - bc$ with the numbers in: that line tells you whether an inverse exists.
